Symptom: Slow WHERE on large table
Keywords: slow query where filter full scan seq scan
Root Cause: Sequential scan despite selective predicate
Strategy: B-tree index on the filtered column(s); composite index ordered by equality-first then range (PostgreSQL 18+: skip scan lets the planner use later columns without a leading-column equality predicate — MySQL has a skip-scan range access since 8.0.13 with narrower conditions, so pre-18 Postgres and most MySQL plans still want equality-first ordering)
Code Good: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at)
Anti-Pattern: Indexing low-cardinality boolean alone; composite ordered range-first
Verification: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) shows Index Scan (PG 18+: or Index Searches for a skip scan); rows estimate ≈ actual — sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-multicolumn.html · https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/range-optimization.html#range-access-skip-scan

Symptom: ORDER BY ... LIMIT slow
Keywords: order by limit sort top n latest
Root Cause: Sort node over the whole table for a top-N query
Strategy: Index matching the ORDER BY direction (including DESC/NULLS) so LIMIT walks the index
Code Good: CREATE INDEX idx_events_created_desc ON events (created_at DESC)
Anti-Pattern: OFFSET pagination for infinite feeds (use keyset)
Verification: Plan shows Index Scan Backward / no Sort node

Symptom: N+1 query loop
Keywords: n+1 loop per row lazy load orm repeated query
Root Cause: Hundreds of identical queries differing only by id
Strategy: Eager-load relations / batch with IN(...) or JOIN; dataloader pattern at the API layer
Code Good: SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id IN (...)
Anti-Pattern: Fixing with a cache instead of the access pattern
Verification: Query count per request flat vs item count

Symptom: LIKE '%term%' search
Keywords: like contains search wildcard fulltext
Root Cause: Leading-wildcard LIKE can't use B-tree
Strategy: Trigram index (pg_trgm GIN) or full-text search (tsvector + GIN); dedicated engine beyond ~10M rows
Code Good: CREATE INDEX idx_users_name_trgm ON users USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops)
Anti-Pattern: Forcing LOWER() without an expression index
Verification: Plan shows Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index

Symptom: JOIN explosion
Keywords: join many tables slow hash join nested loop
Root Cause: Mis-estimated join order / missing join keys index
Strategy: Index every FK used in joins; verify row estimates; break monster joins into CTE/temp stages when estimates collapse (MySQL 9.7: the Hypergraph Optimizer ships in Community Edition but is OFF by default — optimizer_switch reads hypergraph_optimizer=off; switch it on per session or statement to let it choose join order, then verify estimates before assuming a manual rewrite is still needed)
Code Good: ANALYZE tables; index fk columns
Anti-Pattern: Disabling nested loops globally; hint-chasing before stats are fresh
Verification: Estimates within ~10x of actuals at every join node

Symptom: Aggregation over millions of rows
Keywords: group by count sum report aggregate slow
Root Cause: Repeated full-table aggregation for dashboards
Strategy: Pre-aggregate: materialized view / rollup table refreshed on schedule or trigger; partial indexes for hot subsets
Code Good: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_rev AS ... REFRESH CONCURRENTLY
Anti-Pattern: Caching in app memory only (cold-start storms)
Verification: Dashboard reads hit the rollup, not base tables

Symptom: Pagination deep offset
Keywords: offset page 10000 slow deep pagination
Root Cause: OFFSET N scans+discards N rows
Strategy: Keyset/cursor pagination on a unique ordered key
Code Good: WHERE (created_at,id) < (:c,:i) ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC LIMIT 20
Anti-Pattern: Hiding offset behind a 'page' param and capping at 1000 as a fix
Verification: p99 latency flat across page depth

Symptom: Write contention / lock waits
Keywords: deadlock lock wait contention update hot row
Root Cause: Hot-row updates serialize (counters, balances)
Strategy: Row-level design: ledger inserts over UPDATE-in-place; batch with SKIP LOCKED queues; keep transactions short
Code Good: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for workers
Anti-Pattern: Retrying deadlocks blindly without ordering writes
Verification: Lock wait time ~0 under load test; deadlock rate 0

Symptom: Missing/stale statistics
Keywords: wrong plan estimate stale statistics analyze
Root Cause: Optimizer estimates wildly off → bad plans
Strategy: Auto-analyze tuned for big tables; manual ANALYZE after bulk loads; extended statistics for correlated columns
Code Good: CREATE STATISTICS s_dist (dependencies) ON city,country FROM addr
Anti-Pattern: Hinting every query instead of fixing stats
Verification: Plan estimates ≈ actuals after ANALYZE

Symptom: Over-indexing writes
Keywords: insert slow many indexes write amplification
Root Cause: Each extra index taxes every INSERT/UPDATE
Strategy: Audit with index-usage stats; drop unused; covering index to replace several near-duplicates
Code Good: pg_stat_user_indexes idx_scan = 0 candidates
Anti-Pattern: Adding an index per slow query without retiring old ones
Verification: Write p95 recovers; no unused-index rows

Symptom: SELECT * over wide rows
Keywords: select star wide row toast network payload
Root Cause: Fetching unused columns (TOAST/LOB) dominates IO
Strategy: Project needed columns; covering index enables index-only scans
Code Good: SELECT id,status,total FROM orders ...
Anti-Pattern: Compressing payloads instead of trimming the select list
Verification: Plan shows Index Only Scan where applicable

Symptom: JSON column filtering
Keywords: json jsonb attribute filter schemaless
Root Cause: Filtering inside JSON without index = full scan
Strategy: GIN index on jsonb path ops, or generated column + B-tree for hot keys
Code Good: ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN status text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (doc->>'status') STORED; CREATE INDEX ...; -- PG18+: STORED must be explicit (default flipped to VIRTUAL — not indexable)
Anti-Pattern: Stuffing relational data into one JSON blob; relying on the pre-PG18 STORED default
Verification: Plan uses the GIN/generated-column index

Symptom: Many-to-many relationship modeled with an array or id list
Keywords: many to many n-n junction pivot join table association membership users projects role
Root Cause: An n-n relation stored as an array / comma-separated id column (or a duplicated FK) cannot be constrained, indexed per side, or carry attributes of the relationship
Strategy: Junction table with one FK per side and a composite primary key (or unique constraint) over the pair; attributes of the relationship itself (role, joined_at) live on the junction row; add a second index led by the other FK for reverse lookups
Code Good: CREATE TABLE project_members (project_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id), user_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id), role TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (project_id, user_id)); CREATE INDEX idx_project_members_user ON project_members (user_id)
Anti-Pattern: Comma-separated id lists; storing the role on users when it differs per project; a junction table without a uniqueness constraint over the pair
Verification: Inserting the same (project_id, user_id) pair twice fails; EXPLAIN of a lookup by user_id uses idx_project_members_user

Symptom: Relationship cardinality not stated — foreign key nullable by accident
Keywords: cardinality optional mandatory nullable foreign key not null one to many zero or one relationship
Root Cause: Whether the child may exist without a parent was never decided, so the FK column defaults to nullable and orphans accumulate
Strategy: State the cardinality of each side before writing the column: a mandatory parent makes the FK NOT NULL; an optional parent keeps it nullable and the meaning of NULL is documented; 'at least one child' cannot be enforced by an FK alone — enforce it in the application or with a trigger and test it
Code Good: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET NOT NULL  -- PostgreSQL syntax; MySQL: MODIFY the column with NOT NULL
Anti-Pattern: Leaving every FK nullable 'for flexibility'; adding NOT NULL without first counting existing NULL rows
Verification: SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL returns 0 before the constraint; afterwards an insert without a parent fails

Symptom: Status or type stored as unconstrained free text
Keywords: enum status type representation lookup table check constraint native enum closed set
Root Cause: A closed set of states is stored as an arbitrary string, so typos and unknown values are accepted
Strategy: Closed and stable set: constrained column (CHECK constraint, or a native enum type); set that grows, carries attributes (label, sort order) or is edited by users: lookup table plus FK. Native enums are harder to change: PostgreSQL can add enum values but not drop them without recreating the type; a MySQL ENUM list change is an ALTER TABLE — verify the DDL algorithm for your version
Code Good: status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('draft','sent','paid'))  -- MySQL enforces CHECK since 8.0.16
Anti-Pattern: Free-text status with no constraint; a native enum for a set that changes every sprint; a lookup table for two fixed values
Verification: Inserting an unlisted value fails (CHECK or FK violation); the application's enum and the database set are compared in a test — sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/sql-altertype.html · https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/enum.html · https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/create-table-check-constraints.html (CHECK enforced from 8.0.16)

Symptom: Should this foreign key cascade on delete
Keywords: on delete cascade restrict set null referential action invoices payments delete parent child rows
Root Cause: The referential action was left at the default or set to CASCADE everywhere, without deciding what deleting the parent should mean for each child
Strategy: Choose per relation: records with legal or financial weight (invoices, payments) → RESTRICT / NO ACTION and archive the parent instead of deleting; expendable children owned by the parent (draft cart lines, sessions) → CASCADE; very large child sets → delete children in batches before the parent rather than one cascading transaction; SET NULL only when the child stays meaningful without a parent. MySQL note: cascaded FK actions do not fire InnoDB triggers
Code Good: FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT
Anti-Pattern: CASCADE as the default for every FK; deleting a parent with millions of children in one statement
Verification: Deleting a customer that has invoices fails with an FK violation; on a staging copy the row count removed by a cascade matches the expected children

Symptom: UUID or BIGINT primary key
Keywords: primary key type uuid bigint ulid uuidv7 identity auto increment surrogate external id
Root Cause: Random UUIDv4 primary keys scatter inserts across the B-tree (InnoDB also clusters rows by primary key), while sequential ids exposed in URLs leak volume and invite enumeration
Strategy: BIGINT identity as the internal primary key and join key; a separate opaque external id (UUID) with a unique index for URLs and APIs. If the primary key must be a UUID, prefer a time-ordered one (UUIDv7 or ULID) over random UUIDv4 for index locality, stored in a native uuid type (PostgreSQL) or BINARY(16) (MySQL), not CHAR(36)
Code Good: id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, public_id UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE DEFAULT uuidv7()  -- uuidv7(): PostgreSQL 18+
Anti-Pattern: Random UUIDv4 as the clustered key; CHAR(36) UUID storage; exposing auto-increment ids publicly
Verification: EXPLAIN of a lookup by public_id uses the unique index; compare insert throughput and index size of the candidate key types on a load test before committing — sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-uuid.html (uuidv7 from 18) · https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/miscellaneous-functions.html (UUID_TO_BIN)

Symptom: Wide table with rarely read large columns
Keywords: one to one extraction split table wide columns vertical partition profile details rarely read
Root Cause: Hot queries read a narrow subset while large optional columns widen every row
Strategy: Extract the rarely read columns into a one-to-one table whose primary key is also the FK to the parent, so at most one row per parent can exist. PostgreSQL already moves large values out of line (TOAST) — measure before splitting
Code Good: CREATE TABLE user_profiles (user_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, bio TEXT, preferences JSONB)
Anti-Pattern: Splitting columns that are always read together (adds a join to every read); a 1-1 table with its own surrogate id and a nullable FK
Verification: A second profile row for the same user_id is rejected; EXPLAIN of the hot query no longer touches the extracted columns

Symptom: Unique email breaks with soft deletes
Keywords: soft delete deleted_at unique constraint email partial unique index generated column re-register
Root Cause: A plain UNIQUE(email) blocks re-registering a soft-deleted address, and UNIQUE(email, deleted_at) allows duplicate live rows because NULLs compare as distinct
Strategy: Enforce uniqueness only among live rows. PostgreSQL: partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. MySQL has no partial index: add a generated column that holds the email while live and NULL once deleted, and put the unique index on it (a unique index admits multiple NULLs)
Code Good: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_users_email_live ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL  -- MySQL: email_live VARCHAR(255) AS (IF(deleted_at IS NULL, email, NULL)) STORED, UNIQUE (email_live)
Anti-Pattern: UNIQUE(email, deleted_at); checking uniqueness only in application code
Verification: Two live rows with the same email fail; one live row plus one soft-deleted row with that email succeed — sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/indexes-partial.html · https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/create-table-generated-columns.html

Symptom: Foreign key column needs an index in PostgreSQL
Keywords: foreign key index fk column postgres innodb auto index referencing column delete parent slow join
Root Cause: PostgreSQL indexes the referenced (parent) key but not the referencing column, so joins on the FK and every parent DELETE / key UPDATE scan the child table
Strategy: PostgreSQL: create an index on the referencing column(s) when you join on them or delete / update parents. InnoDB requires an index on FK columns and creates one if none exists — check before adding a duplicate; an existing composite index led by the FK column already serves
Code Good: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id)
Anti-Pattern: Assuming PostgreSQL indexed the FK; adding a second single-column index in MySQL where a composite index already leads with the FK
Verification: PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN of a child lookup by the FK shows an index scan; MySQL: SHOW INDEX FROM orders lists an index led by customer_id — sources: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/create-table-foreign-keys.html · https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-FK

Symptom: Myth: a full table scan is always bad
Keywords: full table scan always bad sequential scan seq scan avoid myth index always faster
Root Cause: Treating the plan node type as the problem instead of the measured cost
Strategy: A sequential scan is often the cheapest plan when the query reads a large fraction of the table or the table is small; random index access to many rows can be slower. Judge by actual time and estimated vs actual rows, not by the word 'scan'
Code Good: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ...  -- compare against the forced-index plan in a test session only
Anti-Pattern: Forcing index use with hints or disabling sequential scans in production
Verification: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE for both plans on production-like data (PostgreSQL: SET enable_seqscan = off in a test session only); keep the faster one

Symptom: Myth: put the most selective column first in a composite index
Keywords: most selective column first composite index column order selectivity cardinality myth
Root Cause: Ordering index columns by selectivity alone ignores which predicates and sort the queries actually use
Strategy: Order columns by how queries use them: columns compared with equality first, then the range or ORDER BY column. Selectivity is a tie-breaker among equality columns, not the rule; a leading column the query does not constrain usually makes the index unusable for it (skip scan — PostgreSQL 18, MySQL since 8.0.13 — relaxes this in some cases; verify with EXPLAIN)
Code Good: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at)  -- WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ?
Anti-Pattern: Putting a range column first because it is more selective; one index per column instead of one composite
Verification: EXPLAIN of each real query shows the index used with the expected index condition and no extra Sort node — sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-multicolumn.html · https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/range-optimization.html#range-access-skip-scan

Symptom: Myth: a subquery always becomes a join
Keywords: subquery always join rewrite flatten in exists correlated subquery optimizer myth
Root Cause: Assuming the optimizer rewrites every subquery into a join, or that subqueries are always slow
Strategy: Whether a subquery is flattened depends on its form and on the engine and version: IN / EXISTS often become semi-joins, correlated scalar subqueries may run per outer row, and NOT IN differs semantically from NOT EXISTS when NULLs are present. Check the plan instead of assuming either way
Code Good: SELECT ... FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
Anti-Pattern: Rewriting every subquery as a join by reflex; NOT IN over a nullable column
Verification: EXPLAIN shows a semi-join / hash join or a per-row subplan; compare row counts of NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS on data containing NULLs
Engine: engine-neutral (verify with EXPLAIN for your version)

Symptom: Myth: every foreign key is automatically indexed
Keywords: every foreign key automatically indexed fk index auto created postgres mysql myth
Root Cause: Generalising InnoDB behaviour to every engine
Strategy: Engine-specific: InnoDB requires an index on FK columns and creates one if missing; PostgreSQL does not index the referencing column (only the referenced key has its PK / unique index). In PostgreSQL add the index yourself when you join on the FK or delete parents
Code Good: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id)  -- PostgreSQL
Anti-Pattern: Assuming the index exists after creating the FK in PostgreSQL
Verification: PostgreSQL: list FK constraints whose columns are not the leading columns of any index; MySQL: SHOW INDEX FROM the child table — sources: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/create-table-foreign-keys.html · https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-FK

Symptom: Myth: MySQL and MariaDB are the same
Keywords: mysql mariadb same identical compatible drop-in replacement fork myth
Root Cause: MariaDB began as a fork of MySQL; the two have diverged and behave differently in places
Strategy: Treat them as different engines: features, optimizer behaviour, JSON handling (in MariaDB JSON is an alias for LONGTEXT with a validity check), GTID replication format and system variables differ. Check each feature against the documentation of the engine and version you actually run
Code Good: SELECT VERSION();  -- identify the engine and version before trusting a doc page
Anti-Pattern: Applying a MySQL doc page or tuning guide to MariaDB (or vice versa) without checking
Verification: SELECT VERSION() names the engine; the feature is confirmed in that engine's docs for that version — source: https://mariadb.com/kb/en/json-data-type/ (JSON as a LONGTEXT alias)

Symptom: Myth: every migration can have a down()
Keywords: every migration down rollback reversible migration drop column destructive myth
Root Cause: A down() can restore schema shape but not data that the up() destroyed
Strategy: Destructive steps (dropping a column or table, lossy type changes, backfills that overwrite values) are not reversible by migration code — a down() that recreates an empty column is not a rollback. Make change reversible by design: expand-contract (add, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop later) plus a tested backup / restore path
Code Good: Phase 1: ADD COLUMN new_total; backfill; switch reads. Phase 2 (later release): DROP COLUMN old_total
Anti-Pattern: Writing a down() for a DROP and calling the migration reversible; dropping and adding in one release
Verification: On a copy with data: run up then down then up and compare row counts and checksums of the affected columns

Symptom: Myth: online DDL means zero downtime
Keywords: online ddl zero downtime no lock alter table concurrently instant inplace migration myth
Root Cause: 'Online' describes concurrent DML during most of the operation, not the absence of locks
Strategy: Online DDL still takes short exclusive locks: MySQL online DDL needs an exclusive metadata lock briefly at the start and end; PostgreSQL ALTER TABLE takes locks that queue behind long transactions and then block new queries, and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY waits for existing transactions. It also adds I/O and replication lag. Set a lock timeout, check for long transactions first, and retry
Code Good: SET lock_timeout = '5s'; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ...  -- MySQL: SET SESSION lock_wait_timeout before ALTER TABLE ... ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE
Anti-Pattern: Running ALTER TABLE at peak with no lock timeout; ignoring replication lag on large online rebuilds
Verification: Rehearse on staging under load while monitoring lock waits and replication lag; confirm the algorithm the engine actually chose for your version — sources: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-online-ddl-performance.html · https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/sql-createindex.html#SQL-CREATEINDEX-CONCURRENTLY · https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/explicit-locking.html
